Appendix A A Log-Sobolev inequality and the classical Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process

In this appendix we discuss known classical results for the reader’s convenience: we briefly review the relationship between the isoperimetric inequality for classical Fisher information, the Log-Sobolev inequality, and the rate of convergence to the fixed point for the classical Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup. These arguments were given by Carlen [25] for a particular element of the two-parameter family of Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes. Here we specialize to real-valued random variables, but allow arbitrary parameters in order to illustrate the parallels to the qOU semigroup. We also explicitly discuss the convergence to the fixed point, which is only implicit in [25] but appears to be folklore.

Let f0f_{0} be a probability density on ℝ\mathbb{R} of a real-valued random variable XX. The classical Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (cOU) process, for θ>0\theta>0 and σ>0\sigma>0 is given by the Fokker-Planck equation

∂f∂t=θ​∂∂x​[x​f]+σ22​∂2f∂x2=𝒜θ,σ2​(f).\displaystyle\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}=\theta\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left[xf\right]+\frac{\sigma^{2}}{2}\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x^{2}}={\mathcal{A}}_{\theta,\sigma^{2}}(f)\ . (176)

(Carlen considers the case where θ=1\theta=1 and σ2=1/π\sigma^{2}=1/\pi.) The solution to this equation can be written (in terms of random variables) as

Xt\displaystyle X_{t} =e−θ​t​X0+σ2​θ​1−e−2​θ​t​Z,\displaystyle=e^{-\theta t}X_{0}+\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{2\theta}}\sqrt{1-e^{-2\theta t}}Z\ , (177)

where Z∼𝒩⁡(0,1)Z\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,1) is an independent centered Gaussian random variable with unit variance. The stationary solution f∞f_{\infty} therefore is a centered Gaussian distribution with variance σ2/(2​θ)\sigma^{2}/(2\theta). In particular, (177) implies that the second moments satisfy

𝔼⁡[Xt2]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[X_{t}^{2}] =e−2​θ​t​𝔼​[X02]+(1−e−2​θ​t)​σ22​θ.\displaystyle=e^{-2\theta t}\mathbb{E}[X_{0}^{2}]+(1-e^{-2\theta t})\frac{\sigma^{2}}{2\theta}\ . (178)

We use that the relative entropy between a random variable XX and a centered normal variable Zσ2∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2)Z_{\sigma^{2}}\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,\sigma^{2}) is given by D(X∥Zσ2)=−H(X)+12log2πσ2+12​σ2𝔼[X2]D(X\|Z_{\sigma^{2}})=-H(X)+\frac{1}{2}\log 2\pi\sigma^{2}+\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}\mathbb{E}[X^{2}] as can be verified easily. In particular, the relative entropy between the solution at time tt and the fixed point Zσ2/(2​θ)Z_{\sigma^{2}/(2\theta)} is given by

D(Xt∥Zσ2/(2​θ))\displaystyle D(X_{t}\|Z_{\sigma^{2}/(2\theta)}) =−H⁡(Xt)+12​log⁡π​σ2/θ+θσ2​𝔼​[Xt2].\displaystyle=-H(X_{t})+\frac{1}{2}\log\pi\sigma^{2}/\theta+\frac{\theta}{\sigma^{2}}\mathbb{E}[X_{t}^{2}]\ . (179)

Furthermore, we have the following de Bruijn-type identity:

Lemma 10.

Let {Xt}t≥0\{X_{t}\}_{t\geq 0} be of the form (177), i.e., a solution to the cOU process. Let J⁡(X)=∫|∂f⁡(x)∂x|2f⁡(x)​𝑑xJ(X)=\int\frac{|\frac{\partial f(x)}{\partial x}|^{2}}{f(x)}dx denote the Fisher information of a random variable XX with distribution function ff. Then

dd​t|t=0​H​(Xt)\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0}H(X_{t}) =σ22​J​(X0)−θ.\displaystyle=\frac{\sigma^{2}}{2}J(X_{0})-\theta\ . (180)

Observe that the second summand essentially stems from the fact that entropies transform very simply under rescaling of random variables, namely

In particular, using log⁡x≤x−1\log x\leq x-1, we get

for any A>0A>0. Using inequality (187), it is straightforward to show the following.

Let {Xt}t≥0\{X_{t}\}_{t\geq 0} be of the form (177), i.e., a solution to the cOU process with parameters θ>0,σ>0\theta>0,\sigma>0. Then

Appendix B Tightness of the quantum Fisher information isoperimetric inequality

Consider a one-mode Gaussian thermal state ω𝐧\omega_{\bf n} with mean photon number 𝐧>0{\bf n}>0. Its entropy is

S⁡(ω𝐧)\displaystyle S(\omega_{\bf n}) =g⁡(𝐧)=(𝐧+1)​log⁡(𝐧+1)−𝐧​log⁡𝐧.\displaystyle=g({\bf n})=({\bf n}+1)\log({\bf n}+1)-{\bf n}\log{\bf n}\ . (197)

Under the diffusion semigroup, the state ω𝐧\omega_{\bf n} evolves as

et​ℒ𝗁𝖾𝖺𝗍​(ω𝐧)\displaystyle e^{t{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathsf{heat}}}(\omega_{\bf n}) =ω𝐧t, where 𝐧t=𝐧+2​π​t.\displaystyle=\omega_{{\bf n}_{t}}\ ,\qquad\textrm{ where }\qquad{\bf n}_{t}={\bf n}+2\pi t\ .

In particular, by the de Bruijn identity

J⁡(ω𝐧)=2​dd​t​S​(et​ℒ𝗁𝖾𝖺𝗍​(ω𝐧))|t=0=2​g′​(𝐧)​𝐧t′|t=0=4​π​log⁡(𝐧+1𝐧).\displaystyle J(\omega_{\bf n})=2\,\frac{d}{dt}S(e^{t{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathsf{heat}}}(\omega_{\bf n}))\bigg|_{t=0}=2g^{\prime}({\bf n}){\bf n}^{\prime}_{t}\Big|_{t=0}=4\pi\log\left(\frac{{\bf n}+1}{{\bf n}}\right)\ . (198)

Also,

J⁡(et​ℒ𝗁𝖾𝖺𝗍​(ω𝐧))=4​π​log⁡(1+1𝐧+2​π​t).\displaystyle J(e^{t{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathsf{heat}}}(\omega_{\bf n}))=4\pi\log\left(1+\frac{1}{{\bf n}+2\pi t}\right)\ . (199)

Calculating the right-hand side of the quantum Fisher information isoperimetric inequality (74), we obtain

dd​t|t=0​[12​J​(et​ℒ𝗁𝖾𝖺𝗍​(ω𝐧))]−1\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}\bigg|_{t=0}\Bigl[\frac{1}{2}J(e^{t{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathsf{heat}}}(\omega_{\bf n}))\Bigr]^{-1} =1𝐧⁡(𝐧+1)​log−2⁡(1+1𝐧)→ 1 as ​𝐧→∞.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{{\bf n}({\bf n}+1)}\log^{-2}\left(1+\frac{1}{{\bf n}}\right)\rightarrow\ 1\qquad\text{ as }{\bf n}\rightarrow\infty\ . (200)

Appendix C Tightness of the isoperimetric inequality

Consider a one-mode Gaussian thermal state ω𝐧\omega_{\bf n} with mean photon number 𝐧{\bf n}. From Eq. (198) we know that

J⁡(ω𝐧)=4​π​log⁡(𝐧+1𝐧),\displaystyle J(\omega_{\bf n})=4\pi\log\left(\frac{{\bf n}+1}{{\bf n}}\right)\ , (201)

and that the entropy power of ω𝐧\omega_{\bf n} is given by (cf. (197))

N⁡(ω𝐧)=exp⁡(S⁡(ω𝐧)/1)=(𝐧+1)𝐧+1𝐧𝐧.\displaystyle N(\omega_{\bf n})=\exp(S(\omega_{\bf n})/1)=\frac{({\bf n}+1)^{{\bf n}+1}}{{\bf n}^{\bf n}}\ . (202)

Combining these two expressions, we see that the left-hand side of (115) is

J⁡(ω𝐧)​N​(ω𝐧)=4​π​(𝐧+1𝐧)𝐧​log⁡(𝐧+1𝐧)𝐧+1→ 4​π​e for ​𝐧→∞.\displaystyle J(\omega_{\bf n})N(\omega_{\bf n})=4\pi\left(\frac{{\bf n}+1}{{\bf n}}\right)^{{\bf n}}\log\left(\frac{{\bf n}+1}{{\bf n}}\right)^{{\bf n}+1}{\rightarrow}\ 4\pi e\qquad\text{ for }{{\bf n}\rightarrow\infty}\ . (203)

Appendix D On the convergence rate for Gaussian initial states

In this section we show that for a one-mode Gaussian state ρ\rho the following inequality holds:

dd​t|t=0D(et​ℒμ,λ(ρ)∥σμ,λ)≤−ζD(ρ||σμ,λ)\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0}D(e^{t{\mathcal{L}}_{\mu,\lambda}}(\rho)\|\sigma_{\mu,\lambda})\leq-\zeta D(\rho||\sigma_{\mu,\lambda})\qquad with ​ζ=μ2−λ2>0.\displaystyle\text{ with }\zeta=\mu^{2}-\lambda^{2}>0\ . (204)

Furthermore, this statement is optimal: for any ϵ>0\epsilon>0 there exists a Gaussian state ρ\rho such that

dd​t|t=0D(et​ℒμ,λ(ρ)∥σμ,λ)≥−(ζ+ϵ)D(ρ||σμ,λ).\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0}D(e^{t{\mathcal{L}}_{\mu,\lambda}}(\rho)\|\sigma_{\mu,\lambda})\geq-(\zeta+\epsilon)D(\rho||\sigma_{\mu,\lambda})\ . (205)

First, we note that the entropy of a Gaussian state does not depend on its first moments. Hence it follows that for a Gaussian state the right-hand side of Eq. (151) does not depend on its first moments, and it is suffices to consider centered Gaussian states.

Calculating the right-hand side of (151), we focus on calculating J±​(ρ)J_{\pm}(\rho). Recall that the covariance matrix MM of a centered state ρ\rho is defined as Mj​k=𝗍𝗋⁡(ρ⁡{Rj,Rk})M_{jk}=\mathsf{tr}(\rho\{R_{j},R_{k}\}).

Lemma 11.

Let ρ\rho be a one-mode centered Gaussian state with mean-photon number 𝐧{\bf n} and covariance matrix given by M=κ​ST​SM=\kappa S^{T}S, where κ=2​𝐧+1\kappa=2{\bf n}+1, and S=O1​(z001/z)​O2TS=O_{1}\begin{pmatrix}z&0\\ 0&1/z\end{pmatrix}O_{2}^{T} with Oi∈S​p​(2)∩O⁡(2)O_{i}\in Sp(2)\cap O(2) and z≥1z\geq 1. J±​(ρ)=2​dd​t​S​(et​ℒ±​(ρ))|t=0.\left.J_{\pm}(\rho)=2\frac{d}{dt}S\left(e^{t{\mathcal{L}}_{\pm}}(\rho)\right)\right|_{t=0}\ .

Then we have

J±​(ρ)=(12​(1/z2+z2)±κ)​(log⁡(κ+12)−log⁡(κ−12)).J_{\pm}(\rho)=\left(\frac{1}{2}\left(1/z^{2}+z^{2}\right)\pm\kappa\right)\left(\log\left(\frac{\kappa+1}{2}\right)-\log\left(\frac{\kappa-1}{2}\right)\right)\ . (206)

The covariance matrix of the time-evolved state et​ℒ±​(ρ)e^{t{\mathcal{L}}_{\pm}}(\rho) is

where

c1−​(t)=e−t\displaystyle c_{1}^{-}(t)=e^{-t}\qquad and c2−​(t)=1−e−t,\displaystyle\text{ and }\qquad c_{2}^{-}(t)=1-e^{-t}\ , (208)

Therefore writing S⁡[M]S[M] for the entropy of a Gaussian state with covariance matrix MM, we have

S​[M±​(t)]\displaystyle S\left[M_{\pm}(t)\right] =S[c1±(t)κSTS+c2±(t)id]=S[c1±(t)κO2TKTO1TO1KO2+c2±(t)O2TO2]\displaystyle=S\left[c_{1}^{\pm}(t)\kappa S^{T}S+c_{2}^{\pm}(t)\mathop{\rm id}\right]=S\left[c_{1}^{\pm}(t)\kappa O_{2}^{T}K^{T}O_{1}^{T}O_{1}KO_{2}+c_{2}^{\pm}(t)O_{2}^{T}O_{2}\right] (210)
=S[c1±(t)κKTO1TO1K+c2±(t)id]\displaystyle=S\left[c_{1}^{\pm}(t)\kappa K^{T}O_{1}^{T}O_{1}K+c_{2}^{\pm}(t)\mathop{\rm id}\right] (211)
=S⁡[(c1±​(t)​κ​z2+c2±​(t)00c1±​(t)​κ/z2+c2±​(t))].\displaystyle=S\left[\begin{pmatrix}c_{1}^{\pm}(t)\kappa z^{2}+c_{2}^{\pm}(t)&0\\ 0&c_{1}^{\pm}(t)\kappa/z^{2}+c_{2}^{\pm}(t)\end{pmatrix}\right]\ . (212)

The symplectic eigenvalue of the matrix argument in (212) is the square root of its determinant:

κ±​(t)=(c1±​(t)​κ+c2±​(t)​z2)​(c1±​(t)​κ+c2±​(t)/z2).\kappa_{\pm}(t)=\sqrt{\left(c_{1}^{\pm}(t)\kappa+c_{2}^{\pm}(t)z^{2}\right)\left(c_{1}^{\pm}(t)\kappa+c_{2}^{\pm}(t)/z^{2}\right)}\ . (213)

where g⁡(x)=(x+1)​log⁡(x+1)−x​log⁡xg(x)=(x+1)\log(x+1)-x\log x and 𝐧​(κ)=12​(κ−1){\bf n}(\kappa)=\frac{1}{2}(\kappa-1). By the chain rule, we have that

∎

From Lemma 8 it is clear that we are interested in minimizing J±​(ρ)J_{\pm}(\rho). Both expressions in (206) have a minimum at z=1z=1. Therefore, with ζ=μ2−λ2\zeta=\mu^{2}-\lambda^{2} and 𝐧=κ−12{\bf n}=\frac{\kappa-1}{2}, from Lemma 8 we obtain

−ζD(ρ||σμ,λ)−dd​t|t=0D(et​ℒμ,λ(ρ)∥σμ,λ)≥\displaystyle-\zeta D(\rho||\sigma_{\mu,\lambda})-\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0}D(e^{t{\mathcal{L}}_{\mu,\lambda}}(\rho)\|\sigma_{\mu,\lambda})\geq μ2​log⁡(𝐧+1)−λ2​log⁡𝐧+λ2​log⁡λ2\displaystyle\mu^{2}\log({\bf n}+1)-\lambda^{2}\log{\bf n}+\lambda^{2}\log\lambda^{2} (222)
−μ2​log⁡μ2+(μ2−λ2)​log⁡(μ2−λ2)\displaystyle-\mu^{2}\log\mu^{2}+(\mu^{2}-\lambda^{2})\log(\mu^{2}-\lambda^{2}) (223)

The only solution is 𝐧=λ2μ2−λ2{\bf n}=\frac{\lambda^{2}}{\mu^{2}-\lambda^{2}}, and since

d2d​𝐧2|𝐧=λ2μ2−λ2​hμ,λ​(𝐧)=(μ2−λ2)​(1λ2−1μ2)>0,\displaystyle\frac{d^{2}}{d{\bf n}^{2}}\bigg|_{{\bf n}=\frac{\lambda^{2}}{\mu^{2}-\lambda^{2}}}h_{\mu,\lambda}({\bf n})=(\mu^{2}-\lambda^{2})\left(\frac{1}{\lambda^{2}}-\frac{1}{\mu^{2}}\right)>0\ , (226)

it is the minimum. The value of the minimum is hμ,λ​(λ2μ2−λ2)=0h_{\mu,\lambda}\left(\frac{\lambda^{2}}{\mu^{2}-\lambda^{2}}\right)=0, hence it follows that hμ,λ​(𝐧)≥0h_{\mu,\lambda}({\bf n})\geq 0 for all 𝐧>0{\bf n}>0 and we have

dd​t|t=0D(et​ℒμ,λ(ρ)∥σμ,λ)≤−ζD(ρ∥σμ,λ).\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}\bigg|_{t=0}D(e^{t{\mathcal{L}}_{\mu,\lambda}}(\rho)\|\sigma_{\mu,\lambda})\leq-\zeta D(\rho\|\sigma_{\mu,\lambda})\ . (227)

Moreover, the last inequality becomes equality for ρ=σμ,λ=ω𝐧∞\rho=\sigma_{\mu,\lambda}=\omega_{{\bf n}_{\infty}}, with 𝐧∞=λ2μ2−λ2{\bf n}_{\infty}=\frac{\lambda^{2}}{\mu^{2}-\lambda^{2}}.

It remains to show that ζ=μ2−λ2\zeta=\mu^{2}-\lambda^{2} is optimal. Let ϵ>0\epsilon>0 and ζ′=ζ+ϵ\zeta^{\prime}=\zeta+\epsilon. Then for the Gaussian thermal state ω𝐧\omega_{\bf n} we have

+ϵ​𝐧​log⁡(λ2μ2)+ϵ​log⁡(1−λ2μ2)\displaystyle+\epsilon\,{\bf n}\log\left(\frac{\lambda^{2}}{\mu^{2}}\right)+\epsilon\log\left(1-\frac{\lambda^{2}}{\mu^{2}}\right) (229)
=\displaystyle= log⁡((𝐧+1𝐧)μ2+ϵ⁡(𝐧+1)​𝐧μ2−λ2+ϵ​(λ2μ2)ϵ​𝐧)\displaystyle\log\left(\left(\frac{{\bf n}+1}{{\bf n}}\right)^{\mu^{2}+\epsilon({\bf n}+1)}{\bf n}^{\mu^{2}-\lambda^{2}+\epsilon}\left(\frac{\lambda^{2}}{\mu^{2}}\right)^{\epsilon{\bf n}}\right) (230)

where c⁡(μ,λ)=log⁡((μ2)−μ2−ϵ​(λ2)λ2​(μ2−λ2)μ2−λ2+ϵ)\mathrm{c}(\mu,\lambda)=\log\left((\mu^{2})^{-\mu^{2}-\epsilon}(\lambda^{2})^{\lambda^{2}}(\mu^{2}-\lambda^{2})^{\mu^{2}-\lambda^{2}+\epsilon}\right). Therefore, for any ϵ>0\epsilon>0, there exists 𝐧{\bf n} such that
